podcast.title: False Claim of Buddy Holly Encounter (1955)
podcast.body: Tommy Steele claimed in his autobiography and other sources that he saw Buddy Holly sing "Peggy Sue" on a Grand Ole Opry tour in Norfolk, Virginia, in 1955, which inspired his turn to rock and roll. However, this story is inaccurate; Buddy Holly didn't tour until May 1956 (three months after Hicks left cruise ships), only toured in Oklahoma (a landlocked state), and "Peggy Sue" was not written until 1957. "So, whatever it was that introduced young Tommy Hicks to the wonders of rock and roll, it wasn't seeing Buddy Holly sing Peggy Sue in North of Virginia in 1955."

podcast.title: Brief Number One Hit (1956)
podcast.body: Tommy Steele became the first British rock and roll singer to reach number one in the UK charts with his cover of "Singing The Blues" in late 1956. This was due to a one-week distribution problem for Guy Mitchell's competing version, allowing Steele's version to briefly top the charts before Mitchell's returned to number one. "Tommy Steele had become the first British rock and roll singer to get to number one in the UK charts."

podcast.title: Enduring Popularity (2009)
podcast.body: Despite moving away from rock and roll, his 1950s hits remained popular enough in the UK for a compilation of them to reach number 22 on the charts in 2009. "His 1950s hit remained popular enough in the UK, there's a compilation of them, what's in number 22 in the chart in 2009."

podcast.title: Audition in Men's Toilets
podcast.body: Eager to sign him, Decca Records producer Hugh Mendel did not check for available studios, leading to Tommy Steele auditioning for his record contract in the men's toilets. "Britain's first homegrown rock idol auditioned for his record contract in the Jents toilets."

podcast.title: Discovery Location
podcast.body: Was discovered at The Two I's, a renowned coffee bar and music venue. "the famous coffee bar where the Viper's used to play, and where both Tommy Steel and Terry Dean had been discovered."

podcast.title: Early British Rock and Roll Star
podcast.body: Considered an early, albeit "pre-Elvis," pioneer of British rock and roll. He followed the rockabilly archetype of a young man with a guitar. "Tommy Steele had been a good start, but he'd jumped the gun a little bit."

podcast.title: Early Life and Aspirations
podcast.body: Thomas Hicks came from a dirt-poor background, experienced the death of three siblings at young ages, and suffered from ill health himself, which limited his formal education despite being a voracious reader. From an early age, he wanted to be a performer, developing a routine of miming to Danny Kay records in pubs. "Hicks had come from an absolutely dirt poor background."

podcast.title: Elvis Imitation
podcast.body: He achieved a number one hit by attempting to replicate Elvis Presley's vocal mannerisms, although this imitation was generally not perceived as credible. "when he tried to copy Elvis's vocal mannerisms, while it brought him in number one hit, it didn't really sound particularly credible."

podcast.title: False Claim of Gymnastics Instructor Role
podcast.body: Early in his career, Thomas Hicks claimed to have worked his way up to being a gymnastics instructor on cruise ships, a claim that was denied to the press by the Shipping Federation. "he claimed he'd worked his way up on the cruise ships to being a gymnastics instructor, something that the shipping Federation denied to the press."

podcast.title: Influence on David Bowie
podcast.body: A nine-year-old David Jones (later David Bowie) was inspired to become a rock and roll star after seeing Tommy Steele perform on a tour following the success of "Singing The Blues." Steele's "overly manored, musical inspired, cocknified impression of an American singing style" is seen as a root for Bowie's own London take on Elvis. "On Steele's subsequent tour, a nine-year-old kid called David Jones, who would later change his name to Bowie, went to see him and came away inspired to become a rock and roll star."

podcast.title: Later Career and Longevity
podcast.body: Steele worked on stage with Gene Kelly and on screen with Fred Astaire, wrote several books, pursued a minor artistic career as a sculptor, and toured constantly in pantomimes and musicals. At age 82, he continued to tour yearly, performing as Scrooge in a stage musical version of "A Christmas Carol." "At age 82 he still tours every year, performing a scrooge in a stage musical version of a Christmas Carol."

podcast.title: Merchant Navy Career (age 15)
podcast.body: At age 15, Thomas Hicks joined the merchant navy, working as wait staff on a cruise ship that made regular trips to America. This provided him exposure to American music, notably Hank Williams. "at age 15 he had joined the merchant navy."

podcast.title: Novelty Songs
podcast.body: His early recordings were often novelty songs that incorporated the word "rock," such as "Rock with the Caveman." "His records were still novelty songs with the word rock thrown in, like Rock with the caveman."

podcast.title: Pioneer of British Rock and Roll Industry
podcast.body: The transcript asserts that "without him there would be no British rock and roll industry as we know it, and the rest of this history would be very different." "without him there would be no British rock and roll industry as we know it."

podcast.title: Renamed Tommy Steele
podcast.body: Thomas Hicks was renamed Tommy Steele by his managers, John Kennedy and Larry Parns, as a nod to his paternal grandfather, Thomas Steele Hicks. The spelling of Steele (STIL or STIGL) varies by source. "Hicks was renamed Tommy Steele, in a nod to his paternal grandfather, Thomas Steele Hicks."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Staged High-Society Rock and Roll Show
podcast.body: To generate national attention, John Kennedy rented a large house, hired showgirls, models, and sex workers to attend a party dressed elegantly and using fake posh accents and double-barrelled names. He then invited the press, claiming it was the "first high-society rock and roll show" featuring debutantes. This publicity stunt successfully got Steele national attention. "He then called the press and said it was the first high-society rock and roll show and that the girls were all deputants."

podcast.title: Transition to Light Entertainment
podcast.body: Within a year of his rock and roll success, Tommy Steele moved into light entertainment, starring in films like "The Tommy Steele's Story" and then stage musicals, effectively giving up rock and roll altogether. He eventually became a "national treasure." "Very soon Tommy Steele moved on into light entertainment."
